blocks.text: Functions are fundamental in mathematics and computing, providing a way to map inputs to outputs systematically. Understanding their properties is crucial for problem-solving.

blocks.markdown: In this lesson, we will explore the concept of functions, focusing on their properties such as injectivity, surjectivity, and bijectivity. We will also learn about function composition and the conditions under which a function has an inverse.

blocks.title: Function
blocks.text: A function $f$ from a set $A$ to a set $B$ is a relation that assigns each element of $A$ exactly one element of $B$. We denote this as $f: A \to B$.

blocks.markdown: The set $A$ is called the **domain** of the function, and the set $B$ is called the **codomain**. The set of all images of elements of $A$ is called the **image** of the function.

blocks.title: Injective Function
blocks.text: A function $f: A \to B$ is injective (or one-to-one) if different elements in $A$ map to different elements in $B$. Formally, $f(a_1) = f(a_2)$ implies $a_1 = a_2$ for all $a_1, a_2 \in A$.

blocks.title: Surjective Function
blocks.text: A function $f: A \to B$ is surjective (or onto) if every element in $B$ is the image of at least one element in $A$. Formally, for every $b \in B$, there exists at least one $a \in A$ such that $f(a) = b$.

blocks.title: Bijective Function
blocks.text: A function is bijective if it is both injective and surjective. This means it establishes a one-to-one correspondence between elements of $A$ and $B$.

blocks.title: Checking Injectivity
blocks.prompt: Determine if the function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x) = 2x + 3$ is injective.
blocks.answer: Since $x_1 = x_2$, the function is injective.

blocks.title: Checking Surjectivity
blocks.prompt: Determine if the function $g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $g(x) = x^2$ is surjective.

steps.text: We need to find $x \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $g(x) = y$, i.e., $x^2 = y$.
For $y < 0$, there is no real $x$ such that $x^2 = y$.

blocks.answer: The function is not surjective because negative numbers in $\mathbb{R}$ are not in the image of $g$.

blocks.title: Inverse Function
blocks.text: A function has an inverse if and only if it is bijective. The inverse function reverses the mapping of the original function.

blocks.markdown: Now, let's explore function composition. If $f: A \to B$ and $g: B \to C$, the composition $g \circ f: A \to C$ is defined by $(g \circ f)(a) = g(f(a))$ for all $a \in A$.

points: A function is injective if different inputs map to different outputs.
A function is surjective if every element of the codomain is an image of some element of the domain.
A bijective function is both injective and surjective, allowing it to have an inverse.
Function composition combines two functions into one, with the domain of the composition being the domain of the first function.
